text: The central limit theorem is the reason so much of statistics works. Take many random samples, compute each one's average, and those averages form a bell shape, even when the underlying data looks nothing like a bell. Let's watch it happen.

The collection of sample means is called the sampling distribution of the mean, and the theorem promises three things. Its center is the true population mean. Its spread is the population standard deviation divided by the square root of n. And its shape approaches a normal distribution as n grows, whatever shape the original data had.

We start with a very skewed population: a million simulated order values from an exponential distribution, mean forty. For each sample size, one, five, thirty and a hundred, we draw five thousand samples and average each one. Then we look at those five thousand means.

With n equal to one, the histogram is the skewed population itself. At five it is still lopsided. By thirty it is close to a bell, and at a hundred it is almost perfectly symmetric. The raw data never changed shape. Only the averages did.

The numbers back it up. The mean of the means stays near forty at every size. The spread matches sigma over root n; at thirty, we see seven point two seven against a prediction of seven point three. And skewness falls from one point eight one to zero point two four. Four times the data only halves the spread.

Some fine print. Thirty is a rule of thumb, not a law; very skewed data can need far more. Extremely heavy-tailed data with no finite variance, like the Cauchy distribution, never settles down. And dependent observations, such as clustered customers, break the simple version. The theorem is also about averages, not individual values, which stay skewed.
Up next, standard error, which puts a number on how far a sample mean is likely to stray.
